title: A compass in a Cardan suspension, rocking back towards level
abstract: A compass in a Cardan suspension, rocking back towards level.
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `frame` **(static)** | `point` | `mass = 1`, `position = [0, -0.12, 0]`, `inverse_mass = 0` |
| `ring` | `torus` | `mass = 0.2`, `ring_radius = 0.85`, `tube_radius = 0.035`, `position = [0, 0.12, 0]` |
| `bowl` | `cylinder` | `mass = 2`, `radius = 0.6`, `half_height = 0.05`, `position = [0, -0.12, 0]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`point`** — a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia. `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

**`torus`** — a uniform ring (a doughnut). `I_zz = m (c^2 + 3a^2/4)` about the axis of revolution and `I_xx = I_yy = m (c^2/2 + 5a^2/8)` about any diameter, for ring radius `c` and tube radius `a`. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, which is the axis of revolution — NOT a diameter. Getting those two confused makes a ring that spins invisibly instead of swinging. May also be given as `inner_radius`/`outer_radius`, which is the same ring described from the hole outward.

**`cylinder`** — a uniform solid cylinder. `I_zz = m r^2 / 2` about the axis of symmetry, and `I_xx = I_yy = m (3 r^2 + 4 h^2) / 12` about any diameter. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, like every round shape here. A long thin cylinder is a rod; a short fat one is a disc.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`inverse_mass`** — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.
- **`ring_radius`** — the distance from the torus centre to the middle of its tube.
- **`tube_radius`** — the radius of the torus tube itself.
- **`radius`** — the radius, in metres.
- **`half_height`** — half the height along the cylinder's own z axis.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is OFF** (`g_constant = 0`). The simulator's default is 1, so this had to be said explicitly; without it, bodies that are supposed only to bounce or to be held by joints would also attract each other.
- **Uniform gravity** is `[0, -9.81, 0]` metres per second squared, applied to every body alike.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
- **2 joints** hold the bodies together. A joint is an exact geometric relation held for all time by constraint forces the solver computes — not a stiff spring.
eom:
There are 3 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = m_i g + J^T lambda

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `m_i g` — the uniform field, here `g = [0, -9.81, 0]`
- `J^T lambda` — the constraint forces the joints generate. These are NOT written down by you: they are the Lagrange multipliers, solved for at every step so the joint equations hold exactly

and the torques `T_i` likewise carry a constraint part `J_omega^T lambda`, which is how a bearing resists being twisted out of line.
constraints:
**1. `hinge frame ring [1, 0, 0]` — 5 rows.** The two bodies share a point and an axis: one freedom left, the swing. Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

**2. `hinge ring bowl [0, 0, 1]` — 5 rows.** The two bodies share a point and an axis: one freedom left, the swing. Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

**The arithmetic that decides whether this can be solved at all.** 2 non-static bodies give `6 x 2 = 12` degrees of freedom, against **10 constraint rows**, leaving `12 - 10 = 2` freedoms.

Those remaining freedoms are the motion the mechanism actually has. Some of them may be passive — a freedom nothing applies a force along simply stays where it started.

Every row is held at the position level (`g = 0`) **and** at the velocity level (`d(g)/dt = J u = 0`) at the same time. That is what the GGL formulation is for, and it is why these joints do not slowly come apart.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 3 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
3 bodies x 13 numbers = 39 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

The 1 static body still occupies its 13 slots. Its inverse mass is zero, so its momentum-to-velocity map returns zero and it never moves — carried as constants rather than special-cased out of the layout.

On top of those 39 differential unknowns are the algebraic ones: one Lagrange multiplier `lambda` and one position-level multiplier `mu` for each of the 10 constraint rows, so

```
10 lambda + 10 mu = 20 algebraic unknowns
```

giving **59 unknowns in total**, solved as one implicit system.

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

Because there are joints this is a DAE, and `METHOD IDA` selects the pure-Rust translation of **IDA**. IDA is handed a residual of the implicit form

```
F(t, y, y') = 0
```

built from four blocks: the position rows carrying the `-M^-1 J^T mu` correction, the momentum rows carrying `+J^T lambda`, the rows `g(q) = 0`, and the rows `J u = 0`. IDA runs its variable-order variable-step BDF method and calls back into that residual; the Newton solve at each step is what determines the constraint forces.

**Tolerances.** This model has a joint that grips ORIENTATION, and such a joint imposes a floor of `rtol = 1e-6` and `atol = 1e-8` however tight a tolerance you ask for. That is not timidity: the index-2 accuracy ceiling is real, and asking for more produces convergence failures rather than better answers. Every joint except `CONSTRAIN` grips orientation.

**Consistent start.** A DAE cannot start from an arbitrary state: the start must satisfy `g = 0` and `J u = 0` together. If the initial velocities are not compatible with the joints — a body turning about an offset pivot must have its centre moving — the simulator projects them onto the nearest compatible set and reports how much it changed them.

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set system.g_constant = 0` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `0`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -9.81, 0]` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `uniform_gravity` is a uniform gravitational field applied to every body, as `[gx, gy, gz]` in metres per second squared. This is the everyday 'g' of falling, entirely separate from the mutual attraction above.

The value expected here is `[0, -9.81, 0]`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`collide off` disarms contact detection. Nothing in this model is meant to touch anything else, so leaving it on would have the solver arm a rootfinder hunting for impacts that never happen. The form is `COLLIDE [ON|OFF]`; with no argument it reports the current setting.

It prints the resulting state and the number of collidable pairs.
steps.code:
sim.do("set system.g_constant = 0")
sim.do("set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -9.81, 0]")
sim.do("collide off")

steps.title: Create the bodies
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`new point` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia**, named `frame`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 1` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `position = [0, -0.12, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- `inverse_mass = 0` — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.

Because `inverse_mass` is zero this body is **static**: no force can move it. It is part of the world, not part of the motion.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.

---

`new torus` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform ring (a doughnut)**, named `ring`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I_zz = m (c^2 + 3a^2/4)` about the axis of revolution and `I_xx = I_yy = m (c^2/2 + 5a^2/8)` about any diameter, for ring radius `c` and tube radius `a`. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, which is the axis of revolution — NOT a diameter. Getting those two confused makes a ring that spins invisibly instead of swinging. May also be given as `inner_radius`/`outer_radius`, which is the same ring described from the hole outward.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 0.2` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `ring_radius = 0.85` — the distance from the torus centre to the middle of its tube.
- `tube_radius = 0.035` — the radius of the torus tube itself.
- `position = [0, 0.12, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.

---

`new cylinder` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform solid cylinder**, named `bowl`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I_zz = m r^2 / 2` about the axis of symmetry, and `I_xx = I_yy = m (3 r^2 + 4 h^2) / 12` about any diameter. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, like every round shape here. A long thin cylinder is a rod; a short fat one is a disc.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 2` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `radius = 0.6` — the radius, in metres.
- `half_height = 0.05` — half the height along the cylinder's own z axis.
- `position = [0, -0.12, 0]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.
steps.code:
sim.do("new point as frame { mass = 1, position = [0, -0.12, 0], inverse_mass = 0 }")
sim.do("new torus as ring { mass = 0.2, ring_radius = 0.85, tube_radius = 0.035, position = [0, 0.12, 0] }")
sim.do("new cylinder as bowl { mass = 2, radius = 0.6, half_height = 0.05, position = [0, -0.12, 0] }")

steps.title: Create the bodies (2)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> A torus and a cylinder are both symmetric about their LOCAL z, so both
> are turned to lie FLAT — face onto the vertical. The ring lying flat is
> not a detail: a gimbal ring pivots about a DIAMETER, a line in its own
> plane, so its plane must contain both hinge axes, x and z. Orient it
> instead so its symmetry axis IS the hinge axis and "swinging" becomes a
> spin about its own axis of revolution — which neither shows nor does
> anything, and changes the roll inertia from the diametral
> Mr(c^2/2 + 5a^2/8) to the axial Mr(c^2 + 3a^2/4).

The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set ring.orientation = [0.7071067811865476, 0.7071067811865476, 0, 0]` changes one property of the body `ring` after creation. `orientation` is the attitude, as a unit quaternion `[w, x, y, z]` — **w first**, everywhere in this simulator. Quaternions are used rather than Euler angles because they have no gimbal lock and renormalise cheaply. Setting it renormalises.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set bowl.orientation = [0.7071067811865476, 0.7071067811865476, 0, 0]` changes one property of the body `bowl` after creation. `orientation` is the attitude, as a unit quaternion `[w, x, y, z]` — **w first**, everywhere in this simulator. Quaternions are used rather than Euler angles because they have no gimbal lock and renormalise cheaply. Setting it renormalises.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

steps.title: Declare the joints
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`HINGE` declares a joint. Its form is

```
HINGE <a> <b> <axis>
```

and it contributes **5 scalar constraint equations** to the system, leaving 1 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the two bodies share a point AND an axis: one freedom left, the swing.

Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

Here it is applied to `frame ring [1, 0, 0]`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.

---

`HINGE` declares a joint. Its form is

```
HINGE <a> <b> <axis>
```

and it contributes **5 scalar constraint equations** to the system, leaving 1 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the two bodies share a point AND an axis: one freedom left, the swing.

Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

Here it is applied to `ring bowl [0, 0, 1]`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.
steps.code:
sim.do("hinge frame ring [1, 0, 0]")
sim.do("hinge ring bowl [0, 0, 1]")

steps.title: Choose the integrator
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`method ida` chooses the time integrator. The form is `METHOD <adams|bdf|sprk|ida>`.

Here it selects the pure-Rust translation of **IDA**, SUNDIALS' implicit differential-algebraic solver. Any model with a joint MUST use it, and the simulator refuses every other method for such a model rather than silently integrating an unconstrained problem.

All stepping in this simulator goes through the vendored pure-Rust SUNDIALS translation. There is no hand-written Euler or Verlet anywhere.

steps.title: Create the bodies (3)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> The jolt: a rotation about each hinge axis, which is exactly the
> motion each hinge permits. The linear velocities are the ones those
> rotations imply about a pivot at the origin, v = omega x r, so the
> shared point stays still and g_dot = J u = 0 to roundoff. Set the
> angular velocities without them and the start would be off the
> manifold and would have to be projected first.

The next cell sends these 4 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set ring.angular_velocity = [0.25, 0, 0]` changes one property of the body `ring` after creation. `angular_velocity` is the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set ring.velocity = [0, 0, 0.03]` changes one property of the body `ring` after creation. `velocity` is the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set bowl.angular_velocity = [0.25, 0, 0.3]` changes one property of the body `bowl` after creation. `angular_velocity` is the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set bowl.velocity = [0.036, 0, -0.03]` changes one property of the body `bowl` after creation. `velocity` is the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.
steps.code:
sim.do("set ring.angular_velocity = [0.25, 0, 0]")
sim.do("set ring.velocity = [0, 0, 0.03]")
sim.do("set bowl.angular_velocity = [0.25, 0, 0.3]")
sim.do("set bowl.velocity = [0.036, 0, -0.03]")

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- The values printed above are the result. Read them against the physical expectations set out earlier in this notebook.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

A compass in a Cardan suspension, rocking back towards level.

frame --HINGE x-- ring --HINGE z-- bowl

Two hinges on two perpendicular HORIZONTAL axes: 10 rows on 12
freedoms, leaving the two the suspension exists to give — roll and
pitch. Both axes pass through one point, so the bowl can tilt either
way without its centre going anywhere.

THE DIFFERENCE FROM THE GYROSCOPE GIMBAL is one number: d. There every
centre of mass sat ON the pivot, the lever arm was zero, and gravity
did nothing at all. Here the bowl is PENDULOUS — its centre of mass
hangs d = 0.12 BELOW the pivot — and that is the whole mechanism. A
ship's compass is not held level by its bearings; it is held level by
its own weight, and the bearings only get out of the way.

So gravity is the restoring torque, and each axis is a physical
pendulum with a period you can write down:

T = 2 pi sqrt( I / (M g d) )

pitch, about the inner hinge (z): only the bowl swings.
I = M(3R^2 + 4h^2)/12 + M d^2 = 0.21046667
T = 1.878587 s

roll, about the outer hinge (x): ring and bowl swing together, and the
ring swings about a DIAMETER of itself.
I = 0.21046667 + [ Mr(c^2/2 + 5a^2/8) + Mr d^2 ] = 0.28574980
restoring = (Mb - Mr) g d = 2.11896
T = 2.307339 s

Measured off this recording: 1.883426 s and 2.313653 s, each about
2.7e-3 high. That excess is NOT solver error, it is the finite
amplitude: halve the kick and it falls by 4.01 and 4.02, the signature
of a term in theta^2. Excited on one axis alone the attribution is
exact — the pitch period comes out 4.99e-4 long against a predicted
theta^2/16 = 5.02e-4. With both axes swinging each period is pushed up
by the other's swing as well, so the coefficient is larger.

WHY THE RING SITS ABOVE CENTRE. Every joint pivots at the MIDPOINT of
its pair, so two hinges sharing one point force

p_frame = p_bowl = -p_ring

and a bowl hung d below the centre puts the ring's own centre d above
it. That is what the midpoint rule costs, and it is not cosmetic: the
ring is then top-heavy and SUBTRACTS from the restoring torque, which
is why the roll formula carries (Mb - Mr) and not (Mb + Mr), and why
the ring is made light. Net first moment 2(0.12) - 0.2(0.12) > 0, so
the suspension is still stable, and it seeks level.
